title: Could Nvidia Be the Next Super Micro?
detail:
Could Nvidia Be the Next Super Micro?
David Jagielski, CPA, The Motley Fool
Mon, November 16, 2026 at 12:28 PM CST 4 min read
NVDA
SMCI
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has suddenly become the stock no one wants to buy. Its co-founder, Jensen Huang, has resigned and is no longer the company's president and CEO. The big concern is that Huang has been involved in an affair with a Chinese spy, which has potentially resulted in billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips being sent to China illegally.

The danger is that it could result in legal consequences for Huang and cast a shadow over the company's operations. Investors only need to look as far as another tech company, Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI), as an example of how badly things can get. Its co-founder, Yih-Shyan Liaw, was charged this year in an alleged smuggling scheme to send Nvidia chips to China. And the stock has struggled to rally, even though the business has seemingly done well and grown.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Could Nvidia end up following in the footsteps of Super Micro?

Image source: Getty Images.

There may be similarities, but Nvidia's business is in far better shape

Nvidia's now-former CEO, Huang, hasn't been charged with any crimes. And that may not happen at all. It's too early to tell at this stage just how serious the spy scandal is and if Huang may have played a role in sending unauthorized chips to China.

If, however, that does end up happening, that doesn't mean Nvidia's stock will be as bad a buy as Super Micro has been in recent years. Super Micro has also been the subject of scrutiny over its accounting practices, controls, and procedures; its auditors resigned two years ago amid concerns about its protocols.

Nvidia hasn't come under the same scrutiny. And unlike Super Micro, it generates terrific margins while also growing at a fast rate. With Super Micro, there have been multiple reasons for investors to be concerned about the stock. In Nvidia's case, its financial strength and importance in the tech sector make it much more likely that it'll continue to be a good buy in the long run.

Nvidia remains a promising long-term buy

Based on what's known today, I wouldn't worry about Nvidia's long-term prospects. The business has performed exceptionally well in recent years, its chips are in high demand, and it generates terrific margins on its products. If its former CEO has been involved in an affair that resulted in chips being sent to China, then that's certainly a concerning development, but not one that's likely to cripple the business.

A reported federal smuggling probe is weighing on a major AI server maker, and Washington's widening scrutiny of AI computing flows to China is adding to the pressure. Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) stock recently traded at $25.46, down 5%. That extends a 29% decline for Super Micro stock over the past month.

Shutterstock

Bloomberg reported on November 12. The Department of Justice (DOJ) is investigating whether entities linked to Alice Huang were involved in efforts to smuggle Super Micro products into China. According to that report, the U.S. Attorney's Office in Manhattan leads the inquiry, and U.S. officials suspect Alice Huang has ties to Chinese intelligence. DOJ investigations can conclude without charges, and the reported allegations haven't been tested in court.

Super Micro Answers the Reported Smuggling Probe

Super Micro responded. It said it "has been responsive to inquiries and has fully cooperated with US and Taiwanese officials." The company added that Megaspeed "is not, and has never been, a Supermicro customer."

Export controls were already a sore spot for Super Micro. In its August 11 earnings release, the company disclosed a board-led independent review of certain transactions related to export-control issues. That disclosure means the reported probe lands on a question investors had already been weighing.

Key Takeaways

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent asked whether NVIDIA pushed suspect China sales to "goose" earnings, two days before its Nov. 17 report.

AMD and Supermicro reported strong demand on Nov. 3, after the scandal broke.

Even after HSBC's bear-case cut, the stock trades at about 12x fiscal 2028 earnings.

The test is whether interim CEO Colette Kress keeps next year's outlook.

NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ) reports its third quarter after the close on Tuesday, Nov. 17, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has already asked the question hanging over it. On Fox News's Sunday Morning Futures, he asked: "were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?"

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) and Super Micro Computer (SMCI:NASDAQ) both posted big quarters on Nov. 3, and short seller Culper Research has alleged possible smuggling links between Supermicro, NVIDIA and Megaspeed. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM:NYSE) approved about $40.9 billion of new capacity spending on Nov. 10.

Bessent Wants NVIDIA's Answers in 10 Days

NVIDIA's board accepted Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO on Nov. 11 after revelations of an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based NVIDIA customer US authorities have investigated over suspected chip smuggling to China. That followed a report that the affair helped move $7.5 billion of chips into China. Bessent set a deadline: "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel."

The Risk Is in the Estimates

Consensus has revenue of $412 billion for the fiscal year ending January 2027, nearly double last year's $216 billion, and $689 billion the year after:

NVDA Revenue, Actual and Consensus Estimates: FY2023-FY2028 (TIKR)

Earnings estimates climb from $9.33 a share this fiscal year to $15.85 in fiscal 2028, barely changed from $15.92 on Oct. 23:

NVDA Normalized EPS, Actual and Consensus Estimates: FY2023-FY2028 (TIKR)

HSBC, which downgraded the stock to Hold on Nov. 13, says 11% of revenue over the last six quarters came from countries outside the US and Taiwan, and that tighter export rules could cut fiscal 2028 EPS 13%.

The stock already reflects a lot of that. Its forward P/E is at a five-year low, far below its 36x average:

NVDA Stock NTM P/E: 5-Year (TIKR)

At the Nov. 13 close of $162.85, NVIDIA trades at about 10x fiscal 2028 estimates. Take HSBC's 13% off, and it's still about 12x.

title: Super Micro Is Priced Like It “Goes Bankrupt Next Quarter” Despite $16B of Equity

Super Micro Is Priced Like It "Goes Bankrupt Next Quarter" Despite $16B of Equity ©@Tiero via Canva
Key Takeaways

Super Micro fell 11.3% on Nov. 12 after Bloomberg reported a Justice Department probe into whether its servers were smuggled into China.

The stock trades at 4.3x forward earnings, its lowest in five years, even though analysts expect normalized EPS to jump from $3.63 in fiscal 2026 to $6.52 in fiscal 2027.

Book value is a weak floor: $4.2 billion of Super Micro's roughly $16 billion of equity is preferred stock, inventory alone nearly matches the total, and free cash flow was negative $476 million in the September quarter.

The stock looks too cheap for the earnings analysts expect, and the December-quarter report, expected in early February, is the first test of whether that profit turns into cash.

Shares of Super Micro Computer (SMCI:NASDAQ) fell 11.3% on Nov. 12, closing at $26.99, after Bloomberg reported that federal prosecutors are looking into whether its servers were smuggled into China. They edged down again on Nov. 13, to $26.87, as Nvidia and other tech stocks slipped.

That leaves the stock so cheap that one investor on the r/ValueInvesting subreddit thinks the market has lost the plot. The poster's case is that Super Micro had $16 billion of book equity at the end of last quarter, with no goodwill padding it, and should earn $7 billion over the next year. Yet it trades at a $19 billion market value.

"Seems the market is pricing it goes bankrupt next quarter," the poster wrote.

The earnings math backs that up, at least.

On earnings, it's a bargain

The poster's estimate starts from $80 billion of revenue at a 12% gross margin. That sits inside the $72 billion to $82 billion of fiscal 2027 revenue Super Micro now guides to. It's also close to the 12.7% gross margin the company reported for the September quarter.

Analysts come in lower on the bottom line. Even so, they expect normalized EPS to rise about 80%, from $3.63 in fiscal 2026 to $6.52 in fiscal 2027, the year to June:

Super Micro Computer (SMCI): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2029 (years to June) (TIKR)

Even on those numbers, the stock trades at 4.3x forward earnings. That's its lowest in five years and far below its 14.6x average over that stretch:

Super Micro Computer (SMCI): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

Investors paying 4.3x for rising estimates either doubt the profits will last, or doubt they'll ever show up as cash.

Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) is now answering questions tied to the Megaspeed export-control scandal that has also drawn examination to NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA). The company denies any customer relationship. "Megaspeed is not, and has never been, a Supermicro customer," a Super Micro spokesperson told Fortune on November 13.

24/7 Wall St.

The denial matters because Super Micro builds the servers that carry NVIDIA's GPUs. The U.S. Attorney's Office in Manhattan is reportedly examining whether entities linked to Alice Huang, a former top Megaspeed executive, helped smuggle Super Micro hardware with NVIDIA GPUs into China, according to Fortune. Super Micro and NVIDIA both remain uncharged.

Super Micro Says It Cooperated. Singapore Says Otherwise

The company said it "has been responsive to inquiries and has fully cooperated with U.S. and Taiwanese officials, while also voluntarily providing information and engaging with all requests from Singapore authorities to date." Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said it received only "limited cooperation" and first raised the matter with U.S. authorities on July 7, 2025.

Shares closed at $26.865, down 6.07% over the past week and 23.44% over the past month. NVIDIA fell 12.75% in a week to $162.85.
